title: Gentle Exercises for (Lower) Back Pain
intro: For common lower back pain, light and slow movement often helps more than lying down all day. The moves below focus on gentle stretches and strengthening the muscles that support your spine.
muscles: Deep stomach muscles (core), butt (glutes), lower back muscles and hips. These muscles help support your lower back when you sit, lift things and walk.
steps: Lie on your back with your knees bent. Flatten your lower back against the floor by tightening your stomach slightly. Hold for 3 seconds, then release. Do this 8-10 times.
Still lying down, slowly hug one knee to your chest and hold for 15 seconds. Switch legs. Do this 2 times on each leg.
Get on all fours (hands and knees on the floor). Slowly arch your back upwards, then let it dip down slightly (cat-cow). Do this 8 times within a comfortable range.
Still on all fours, stretch one arm forward, hold for 3 seconds, then switch. Once comfortable, add the opposite leg. Do this 6 times on each side.
Lie on your back with your knees bent. Lift your hips slightly (bridge), hold for 2 seconds, then lower down. Do this 8 times.
mistakes: Doing the moves with jerking or too fast. All moves should be slow and gentle.
Forcing the stretch until it hurts. A bit of tightness is okay, sharp stabbing pain is not okay.
Sitting for long periods without getting up. Getting up and walking for 2-3 minutes every 30-60 minutes helps a lot.
easier: Do only the pelvic tilt and knee hug first. If lying on the floor is hard, do them on a bed that isn't too soft.
harder: Hold the bridge and the arm-leg move longer (5 seconds). Add a 10-15 minute walk after the session.
dose: 1-2 sets of each move, every day or 4-5 times a week. Each session takes about 8-12 minutes.
safety: Stop if the pain gets sharper or spreads down your leg. See a doctor immediately if you have numbness in your legs or groin area, your legs become weak, you have trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or the pain started after a fall or accident.

faq.q: Should I rest or keep moving when my lower back hurts?
faq.a: For common lower back pain, many people feel better faster when they keep moving lightly within a comfortable range. Full rest for days can make your body stiffer. If unsure, ask a doctor or physiotherapist.

faq.q: Can I do sit-ups to strengthen my lower back?
faq.a: Full sit-ups may not be suitable while your lower back is hurting. Moves like the pelvic tilt, bridge and arm-leg on all fours are gentler to start with.

faq.q: Why does sitting long at the office make my lower back hurt?
faq.a: Sitting in one position for a long time can make your muscles tired and stiff. Try setting a reminder to get up, stretch and walk for a bit every hour.
